title: Greed in the shop
tomorrow: it's 2am and Simran's phone is still in her hand. who's holding whom?

lines: SOCKS, A STOOL, A WATER BOTTLE.
cards: Bebe needs a few things for her stay: a shower stool, grippy socks, a bigger water bottle. Simran and Maya go with Maya's grandma, Ruth, who has a coupon for everything.
Somewhere between the socks and the checkout, Simran's cart fills: a candle, a hoodie on sale, earbuds she doesn't need because hers work fine.
Ruth looks at the cart, smiles, and quotes her Bible: 'But godliness with contentment is great gain.' Then Simran's phone buzzes. It's Bebe: bas. Just the socks.

teach.h: LOBH: THE NEXT WANT, LIKE WAVES.
teach.b: So here's the question: how much is enough? The Sikh name for the thief is lobh, greed. On ang 1358, Guru Arjan speaks to it, in paraphrase: O greed, you cling even to the great and toss them about like waves.
The waves are the point. Greed isn't one big want; it's the next one, and the next. Sikh teaching answers with santokh, contentment.

teach.h: SANTOKH: A THREAD HOLDING THE WORLD.
teach.b: In the Japji, on ang 3, Guru Nanak pictures dharma, born of compassion, holding the earth in place, tied with the thread of contentment. Contentment isn't a shrug. It's a thread that holds the world together.

It comes from Paul's first letter to Timothy, chapter six, and the next verse says: 'For we brought nothing into this world, and it is certain we can carry nothing out.' So here's one thing two neighbors share: the Guru Granth and Paul's letter both treat contentment as real wealth, and the restless wanting as a trap.
For Paul, contentment sits beside godliness, a life given to God in Christ. In the Japji, contentment is the thread that holds the world, and the cure for greed is remembering the Name.
Two homes, one shared word, and neither one has to become the other for the word to be true.
Simran puts back the candle, the hoodie and the earbuds. She keeps the socks, and one thing Bebe didn't ask for: a packet of chili seeds for the garden.

how: Sikhs name greed (lobh) among the five thieves and contentment (santokh) among the virtues; the Japji, recited in the morning, pictures contentment as the thread that holds the world.

games.q: what does “greed in the shop” mean?
o: wanting more than you need, one more thing at a time
saving money so you never have to share it
a store's way of tricking shoppers into buying

games.q: the sale ends tonight. you've got what you came for, plus three things you like but don't need. what fits today's idea?
o: keep what you came for and put the rest back.
buy them now, since you'll save money later.
buy one, as a reward for being careful.
games.why: greed is the next want, and the next, like waves. Simran kept the socks, put back the rest, and added chili seeds for Bebe.

practice: Look at one thing you own and use every day: a mug, a pen, a pair of shoes. Notice that it does its job, today, completely. Let the word enough rest on it while you breathe, and for the sit, want nothing more from it.

wordCard.voice: Greed in the shop. Lobh, the thief that always wants the next thing, and santokh, contentment, the thread that says enough.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: santokh, contentment, the thread in the Japji that holds the world in place.

carryVoice: Enough: two old books, one checkout, and the socks were all Bebe needed. See you soon.
